title: Building: data in lists and files
specPoints: 2.2.3 Additional programming techniques: **arrays/lists** (one- and two-dimensional), **records** to store data
2.2.3 **File handling**: open, read, write, close; **string manipulation** (`split`, `strip`, concatenation)
Practical programming skills (Section B): store, search, add, delete and update records and keep a file in step with the data
learn: Choose between parallel lists and a list of lists for a set of records, and justify the choice
Load records from a text file into a list of lists, converting each field to the right type
Save a list of lists back to a file in the same format, one record per line
Implement add, delete, update and search on the list and keep the file in sync
Handle the edge cases: empty file, missing file, record not found
hook: Close the club register and open it again: every member has gone. A program whose data lives only in memory forgets everything when it stops. Today the register gets a memory — a text file — and you learn the pattern that every file-backed program uses: load at the start, work on the list, save at the end.

video.title: Load, work, save
video.brief: 4 minutes. A text file `members.txt` with four lines. Each line is split at the commas and becomes a small list; the small lists stack into a list of lists — an animated table. Add a row, change a number, delete a row — the table changes, the file does not. Then save: each inner list joins back into a line and the file updates. Side panel: the same data as three parallel lists, with an arrow showing the danger when one list is changed and the others are not.

explain.h: Parallel lists or a list of lists?
p: A **record** is one member: name, year, points. Two ways to store many records. **Parallel lists** keep one list per field — `names[2]`, `years[2]` and `points[2]` all belong to member 2. **A list of lists** keeps one inner list per member — `members[2]` is `["Alan", 9, 7]`. OCR questions often use parallel arrays, so you must be able to read them. For your own programs a list of lists is safer: adding or deleting a member changes **one** thing, and you cannot leave the lists out of step.
explain.code:
Parallel lists                      List of lists (2D)
names  = ["Ada", "Grace", "Alan"]    members = [["Ada", 9, 12],
years  = [9, 10, 9]                            ["Grace", 10, 30],
points = [12, 30, 7]                           ["Alan", 9, 7]]

Alan's points:  points[2]           members[2][2]
Add a member:   3 appends           1 append
Delete member 1: 3 pops (easy to forget one)   members.pop(1)
Field names:    the list name says  position says: [0]=name [1]=year [2]=points

p: The file stores one record per line with fields separated by commas: `Ada,9,12`. Loading means: open, read each line, `strip()` the newline, `split(",")` into fields, **cast** the numbers (everything read from a file is text), and append the record. The two edge cases are an **empty line** (skip it) and a **missing file** (start with an empty list rather than crash — `try/except FileNotFoundError` or check first).

Saving is the mirror image: open in **write mode** `"w"` (which replaces the old contents), and for each record join the fields back with commas and write the line with `\n`. Numbers must be turned back into strings. Because `"w"` wipes the file, save writes the **whole list** every time — that is what keeps the file in step with memory. Never use `"a"` (append) for this: after deleting a member, appending would put the deleted member back.

explain.h: Search, add, delete, update — on the list
p: All four operations work on the **list in memory**, not the file. Search loops through the list and returns an index or -1. Add appends a new inner list. Delete `pop`s at the found index. Update changes one field at the found index, e.g. `members[i][2] = members[i][2] + 10`. Then the file is written once, at the end — or, for extra safety, after every change, so a crash loses nothing. Both are acceptable; what the exam wants to see is that the file and the list end up the same.

list: **Parallel lists**: one list for names, one for years, one for points. Item 2 in each list belongs together.
**List of lists**: each member is a small list `[name, year, points]`. Easier to add and delete.
For each line: strip it, split at commas, turn the numbers into `int`, add the record to the list.
If there is no file, start with an empty list.
Open the file with `"w"` — this empties it.
Write every record as one line: `name,year,points`.
Now the file matches the list.

keyterms.def: One set of related fields about one thing, e.g. a member's name, year and points.
Several lists where the items at the same index belong to the same record.
A list whose items are themselves lists, e.g. one inner list per record.
Converting a value from one data type to another, e.g. `int("12")` after reading text from a file.
Opening a file with `"w"`, which replaces its contents; `"a"` (append) adds to the end instead.
Keeping data in a file so that it still exists after the program ends.

try.title: 1. Load and inspect
p: Run it and read the output. Then: (a) print only the names; (b) print the total points; (c) explain to a partner what the line `if line != ""` protects against (hint: files often end with a blank line). (d) Change the filename to `nobody.txt` and run again: it must not crash.
try.code:
def load_members(filename):
    members = []
    try:
        with open(filename) as f:
            for line in f:
                line = line.strip()
                if line != "":
                    fields = line.split(",")
                    members.append([fields[0], int(fields[1]), int(fields[2])])
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print("No file yet - starting with an empty register")
    return members

members = load_members("members.txt")
print(members)
print("Number of members:", len(members))
print("Second member's name:", members[1][0])
print("Second member's points:", members[1][2])

try.title: 2. Save, and prove the file matches
p: Complete `save_members`. Then run: the program loads, awards Tim 25 points, adds a member, deletes Alan, saves, and loads again into a **second** list. The last line must print `True` — the reloaded list is identical to the one in memory. Look at the file contents shown after the run.

try.title: 3. The register with a real file
p: Plug load and save into the menu program. Complete the four TODOs: `add_member` must append a record and save; `award_points` must update and save; `remove_member` must delete and save; option 6 must save and quit. Test: add `Mo` (year 11); award Ada 10; remove Alan; show all; quit. Then run the program **again** and choose 1 — your changes must still be there.

try.title: 4. Read the parallel-array version
p: Exam questions often give parallel arrays. This program uses them for the same register. Run it. Then (a) write a comment next to each line of `remove` saying why all three `pop` calls are needed; (b) delete one of the `pop` lines, run, and describe what has gone wrong with the data; (c) write one sentence comparing the two ways of storing records, mentioning both.

try.title: 5. Save v3
instructions: Save Try 3 as `club_v3.py`. Create `members.txt` next to it with the four sample lines. Run it twice to prove the data persists.
Add a comment at the top: 'Data: list of lists [name, year, points]; file: members.txt one record per line.'

check.q: After reading `"Ada,9,12"` from a file and splitting it, `fields[1]` is:
check.fb: Everything from a file is text until you cast it.

check.q: Saving the whole list with mode `"w"` is correct because:
opts: It replaces the file so deleted records do not come back
check.fb: The file becomes exactly the list.

check.q: A danger of parallel lists is:
opts: Deleting from one list but not the others puts the data out of step
check.fb: Three pops needed; forget one and indexes no longer line up.

check.q: When the data file does not exist yet, the program should:
opts: Ask the user to type the file

exam.q: A file `stock.txt` stores one product per line in the form `name,quantity`. Write a program that reads the file into two arrays, `names` and `quantities`, and then outputs the name of every product with a quantity below 5.
model: File opened for reading (1). Loop reading each line until the end of the file (1). Line split at the comma; name appended to `names` and quantity cast to integer and appended to `quantities` (1). Loop through the arrays comparing each quantity with 5 (1). Name at the same index output when quantity < 5 (1).
exam.commentary: Parallel arrays are given by the brief, so use them. The casting mark is lost if the quantity is compared as a string; the output mark needs `names[i]`, not the quantity.

exam.q: A program stores members in a 2D array and saves it to a file when the user quits. A user adds three members and then the program crashes before quitting. Describe the problem and how the program should be refined.
model: The three new members are lost because the file is only written on quit / the file is out of step with the data (1). Save the array to the file after every add (and delete/update), or write each new record immediately (1).
exam.commentary: Problem then refinement. Students who say 'add error handling' miss the point — the fix is to save more often.

exam.q: Give **one** advantage of storing records in a 2D array rather than in parallel 1D arrays.
model: Any one: adding or deleting a record changes only one structure so the fields cannot get out of step; all the fields of a record are kept together; a whole record can be passed to a subprogram as one value (1).
exam.commentary: Must be a genuine advantage of the 2D version. 'It uses less memory' is not true and does not score.

home: Add a 'Report' option to `club_v3.py` that writes `report.txt`: one line per member sorted by points (highest first) and a final line with the total. Use `"w"` mode. Explain in a comment why `"a"` would be wrong here.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 3 · explain 12 · try 33 · check 4 · exam 5 · homework 3
misconceptions: Forgetting that file data is text: `"30" + 10` crashes, `"30" > "7"` is False.
Using append mode to save, so the file grows with duplicates and deleted records return.
Trying to edit the file directly instead of editing the list and rewriting the file.
Forgetting `strip()`, so the last field is `"12\n"` and `int()` works but a name comparison fails.
say: 'Load at the start. Work on the list. Save the list.'
'What type is it after split? Text. All of it. Cast it.'
'Shut the program and open it again. Is your data still there? Then it persists.'
teacher.skip: Try 4 can be reading homework; Try 2 → Try 3 is the build.
differentiation: Support: give `save_members` complete in Try 2; students do the three TODOs in Try 3.
Stretch: make `load_members` report the line number of any line that does not have exactly three fields and skip it, instead of crashing.
